title: Effects of cis-regulatory elements on proteome
projectDescription: Background Genomic variations contribute to the phenotypic diversity of individuals. A number of polymorphisms in protein-coding regions that alter drug efficacy or lead to adverse reactions have been characterized; however, noncoding regions that affect drug responses are largely overlooked, except for a limited number of well-studied enhancers. Results We conducted a quantitative assessment of cis-regulatory elements (CREs) based on transcription initiation profiling of mRNAs and noncoding RNAs, including enhancer RNAs, by using CAGE (Cap Analysis of Gene Expression). Candidate CREs identified in a hepatocellular carcinoma HepG2 cell line with stable expression of drug-responsive transcription factor pregnane X receptor (PXR) were further narrowed down by integrating data of PXR-binding sites in human primary hepatocytes and genome-wide association studies. We found more than 100-fold enrichments of the candidates to genetically associated loci with circulating levels of bilirubin and vitamin D, which implicated a link to adverse reactions of PXR ligands. We uncovered novel enhancers of UGT1A1 and TSKU through CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments. We identified alleles altering regulatory activities of UGT1A1 and CYP24A1enhancers by using luciferase reporter assay. Furthermore, our siRNA experiments revealed an unexpected impact of TSKU on the expression of vitamin D-metabolizing enzymes. Conclusions Our transcriptome-based assessment of CREs expanded the list of drug-inducible and PXR-mediated enhancers and super-enhancers. We identified regulatory alleles that alter drug-induced gene expressions, and discovered a novel molecular cascade associated with an adverse reaction. Our results contribute a precise understanding of the noncoding elements of the human genome underlying drug responses.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Sample preparation for LC-MS/MS analysis The cell pellets were lysed in 5% sodium dodecyl sulfate, 50 mM tetraethylammonium bromide (TEAB) by sonication. After the resulting proteins were quantified using BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 30 µg of proteins was incubated in 4.5 mM dithiothreitol at 55 °C for 30 min and then cooled to room temperature, followed by alkylation with 10 mM iodoacetamide in the dark for 15 min. Afterwards, final concentration of 2.5% phosphoric acid and six volumes of S-Trap binding buffer (90% methanol, 100 mM TEAB, pH 7.5) were added. This protein lysate was used for S-Trap (PROTIFI) digestion. The protocol was performed the manufacturer’s instructions with minor adjustments. Briefly, the protein lysate was spun through the S-trap micro-spin column and washed 4 times with S-Trap buffer. Finally, 50 mM TEAB with 3µg of Trypsin/Lys-C protease mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) is added and the sample is incubated for 1h at 47℃. The tryptic peptides were sequentially eluted using 40 μl of 50 mM TEAB, 0.5% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and 50% acetonitrile (ACN) and 0.5% TFA. The solution is vacuum centrifuged to almost dryness and resuspended in 0.1% TFA and subjected to peptide quantification (Thermo Fisher Scientific).  Nano-flow liquid chromatography-ion trap mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) Data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) analysis was performed on a Vanquish Neo LC system coupled to a Orbitrap Exploris 480 (both Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides (500 ng) were injected into the packed nano-capillary column Aurora Ultimate (0.075 mm I.D. × 250 mm L, particle diameter 1.7 μm, Ionoptics) at a flow rate of 300 nL/min using the following gradient: 1 min, 2.5% B; 2min, 6% B; 60.3 min, 21% B; 82.6 min, 31% B; 95.6 min, 44% B; 99.6 min, 95% B;104.6 min, 95% B (Buffer A: 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water, and buffer B: 80 % ACN, 0.1 % FA in water). Column temperature was maintained at 55 °C using a column oven (Reifycs Analytical). For ionization, a spray voltage of 1.8 kV and an ion transfer tube temperature of 275°C were used. Full MS scans were acquired at 60k orbitrap resolution from 380–985 Da and a maximum injection time of 25 ms. The MS2 was performed over a mass range of 380–980 Da using 10 Da windows with an overlap of 1 Da.
dataProcessingProtocol: DIA raw data was processed using library-free analysis in DIA-NN 1.9.1.
